chunks.content: KEY POINTS Question : How important are the perceived urgency and barriers for seeking emergency medical care (EMC) for sepsis? Findings : In a nationwide survey with 1013 persons in Germany, perceived urgency was found to be the strongest predictor of seeking EMC. The likelihood of seeking EMC was significantly lower for sepsis-related emergencies (–14.9%) than for nonsepsis-related emergencies, even when controlling for perceived urgency. Meaning : While barriers play a secondary role in the decision to use EMC, the decisive factor is the perceived urgency of the emergency, which, in the case of sepsis, also depends on knowledge of the disease. Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency caused by a dysregulated host response to an infection ( ). Every year, around 50 million patients are affected, of which 11 million die ( ). Sepsis often presents with unspecific early symptoms, such as dyspnea or altered mentation ( ). This can make the early diagnosis of sepsis challenging for both patients and healthcare providers, potentially leading to delays in medical treatment ( ). In an U.S.-wide study including 21 emergency medical services (EMS) agencies in Pennsylvania between 2010 and 2012, the median time from first medical preclinical contact to antibiotic administration in the emergency department (ED) was 4.2 hours (interquartile range, 2.7–8.0 hr) ( ). With each hour of delay in antibiotic administration, the adjusted odds ratio for death increased by 3% per hour ( p < 0.01) ( ). In a German multicenter study, the sepsis mortality risk increased by 2% per hour delay of antimicrobial therapy and 1% per hour delay of source control ( ). However, delays and barriers to sepsis recognition do not begin at the healthcare facility but rather with the patient’s decision or the families/caregivers advice to seek emergency medical care (EMC) ( – ). In a previous survey among sepsis risk groups, we found that most patients would not use EMC in sepsis-related emergencies presented in case vignettes ( ). Compared with other medical emergencies such as stroke and acute myocardial infarction (AMI), respondents more frequently decided that they would wait or consult their general practitioner (GP) ( ). Although this can have important implications for sepsis treatment, we lack knowledge on what affects the decision making of sepsis patients to seek EMC. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that the decision to use emergency and urgent care services was influenced by the following factors in general: access to and confidence in primary care; perceived urgency/need for EMC; and barriers (costs, location) and advice from family, friends, or healthcare professionals ( ). For AMI and stroke, the perception that the symptoms were unrelated to an important health problem ( ) and the failure to recognize the urgency of symptoms ( ) were identified as most important barriers to the timely utilization of EMS in two previous survey studies from Italy and Korea. We hypothesized that these factors may also be important in sepsis, thus building on our earlier survey ( ), the present study extends this work by using a population-representative sample, directly assessing urgency for each vignette, and explicitly capturing potential barriers to seeking EMC. These advances allow us to provide more generalizable insights and to test: 1) if the perceived urgency of sepsis-related emergencies differs from other medical emergencies, 2) if sepsis knowledge and patient demographics are associated with the perceived urgency in sepsis-related emergencies, and 3) what facilitates and hinders seeking EMC in sepsis-related and other emergencies. METHODS Study Design We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional, representative survey study, which was carried out by the Institute for Demoscopy (IfD) Allensbach from December 1–14, 2023. The IfD regularly conducts omnibus surveys on various topics. As part of the IfD survey number 12079, a representative sample of the German population 16 years old or older was interviewed. The sample was drawn using quota sampling. Quotas were determined based on official statistical data for the German population 16 years old or older. Remaining disproportionalities were resolved by weights, which were calculated based on combinations of age and gender, level of education and region (former East and West Germany), occupational group and region, and household size, marital status, Nielsen areas ( ), town size, and voting intention (political party). The study was approved by institutional review board of the Jena University Hospital (Reg.-Nr. 2025-3798-Bef, study title: “Representative Survey on Sepsis Knowledge in the German Population”) and was conducted in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration 1975. Standardized interviews were conducted face-to-face by one of trained 318 interviewers. On average, each interviewer recruited 3–5 participants. Informed consent was not required from participants under data protection law, as the data were processed, evaluated, and passed on in anonymized form. Interviewers signed to confirm appropriate interview conduct in accordance with legal regulations. We followed the Consensus-Based Checklist for Reporting

Standardized interviews were conducted face-to-face by one of trained 318 interviewers. On average, each interviewer recruited 3–5 participants. Informed consent was not required from participants under data protection law, as the data were processed, evaluated, and passed on in anonymized form. Interviewers signed to confirm appropriate interview conduct in accordance with legal regulations. We followed the Consensus-Based Checklist for Reporting of Survey Studies checklist ( ) to present the study results. Questionnaire The questionnaire was constructed based on previous studies ( ) (W. Abels, unpublished observataions, 2025) and consisted of 15 questions on sociodemographic information, 60 questions on sepsis knowledge, ten case vignettes describing medical emergencies and a question on barriers for seeking EMC ( Supplement , https://links.lww.com/CCM/H850 ). Variables Concerning sociodemographic data, we recorded age, gender, region, and educational level. Educational level was defined by categorizing the educational degrees of Germany (low: 8–9 yr of school; intermediate: 10 yr of school; and high: university entrance qualification or university degree). The region reflects whether a participant lives in former East or West Germany. We also recorded if participants themselves or individuals within their social environment had been affected by sepsis. Sepsis Knowledge We assessed five domains of sepsis knowledge: definition and epidemiology (16 items), risk factors (15 items), symptoms (16 items), general prevention (three items), and sepsis sequelae (ten items). We used binary indicator variables to code item responses as 1 = correct and 0 = incorrect. An overall score was calculated as sum score of the indicator variables (i.e., the number of correctly answered items) as measure of sepsis knowledge. The score was calculated only for participants familiar with the term “sepsis”; those unaware received a missing value. Urgency Ratings of Medical Situations and Intended Actions We assessed urgency ratings and intended actions for different medical emergencies using ten case vignettes, each representing a clear indication for EMC according to medical guidelines ( , ). These case vignettes included typical emergencies, of which five were sepsis-related (e.g., sepsis caused by urinary tract infection, sepsis caused by respiratory infection) and five were nonsepsis-related (e.g., AMI or stroke). Participants were asked to rate the urgency of the medical situations on a five-point Likert scale from 1 = very low to 5 = very high. Furthermore, they had to choose one of three possible courses of action (1 = “Call the EMS or go to the ED immediately,” 2 = “Visit the GP on the same day or the outpatient emergency service of the association of statutory health insurance physicians,” and 3 = “Wait 1 day and then decide”). In Germany, if patients suffer from an emergency, they are supposed to either call EMS (calling 112 and receiving on-site-care or care during transportation to a hospital) or to directly visit an ED. In case of less urgent cases and out-of-office hours of the outpatient doctors, patients are supposed to call the so-called “ärztliche Bereitschaftsdienst” (outpatient emergency service of the association of statutory health insurance physicians) or to visit the “on duty practices.” For statistical analysis of the intended action, we created a binary variable to reflect the use of EMC, with the response option “Call EMS immediately or go to the ED” coded as “1” and the other two options coded as “0.” <italic toggle="yes">Barriers for Using the EMC</italic>. Unrelated to specific barriers, we assessed possible subjective barriers for EMC use. Respondents were asked to decide on twelve possible barriers (e.g., concerns about possible costs, long waiting time in the ED, responsibility for children or pets) whether they apply to them (coded as yes = 1 or no = 0). Statistical Analyses To compare whether the urgency rating and intended action differed between the sepsis-related emergencies and the nonsepsis emergencies, we calculated the mean and sd s for the urgency rating and the relative frequencies of the possible intended actions for each case vignette. We analyzed in a multiple linear regression how the urgency rating of sepsis-related emergencies is related to sociodemographic characteristics, sepsis knowledge, and previous experience with sepsis. In addition, we used a multiple linear regression to examine how the tendency to use EMC is associated to the urgency rating, sociodemographic characteristics, possible barriers, and the type of emergency (sepsis-related vs. nonsepsis-related). For both regression analyses, we calculated the mean for the tendency to use EMC and the urgency rating separately across the five sepsis-related and nonsepsis-related case vignettes for each person. For both regression analyses, we calculated the mean for the tendency to use EMC and the urgency rating separately across the five sepsis-related and nonsepsis-related case vignettes for each person. For a person who chooses the option “Call EMS immediately or go to the ED” in three of five nonsepsis-related medical situations, this results in a value of 0.6 for the tendency to use EMC. We reported R 2 differences as measure for the unique explained variance in the regression models. Factorial weighting was used to adjust for remaining deviations of the sample structure of the realized quota sample from official population statistics. Accordingly, statistical methods for complex survey data with sampling weights were used to ensure correct statistical inference ( , ). All statistical analyses were performed with the R package “survey” v.4.4-2 ( ) in the software R v.4.2.3. (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). We report unadjusted p values of statistical tests with a significance level of α = 0.05. We used “listwise deletion” to handle missing data. As none of the variables had a proportion of missing data of more than 5 %, no significant bias is to be expected ( ). RESULTS In total, 1013 persons participated in the survey. The mean age and sd of the participants was 51.2 ± 6.5 years, and 48.6% of the participants were male ( Table ). Almost all participants (95.1%) had previously heard the term “sepsis.” The mean overall sepsis knowledge score across all domains was mean = 29.9 of 60 ( sd = 6.5). Thus, on average, people achieved just half of the maximum possible points in the overall sepsis knowledge. The descriptive comparison of the urgency rating and the intended action in sepsis-related and nonsepsis-related emergencies revealed that nonsepsis-related emergencies were rated as more urgent and the response option “Call the EMS or go to the ED immediately” was selected more frequently ( Table ). The mean urgency rating over all sepsis-related emergencies was significantly ( t = 12.5; degrees of freedom = 1011; p < 0.01) lower (mean = 3.93; sd = 0.64) than that of nonsepsis-related emergencies (mean = 4.15; sd = 0.67). In sepsis-related emergencies, the response category “Call the EMS or go to the ED immediately” was selected by a minority of participants (between 18.3% and 43.2% of respondents). In contrast, in nonsepsis-related emergencies, this category was the preferred option in most vignettes (between 20.1% and 71.9%). This pattern reverses when considering the category “Visit the GP on the same day or the outpatient emergency service of the association of statutory health insurance physicians.” For all sepsis-related emergencies, the majority of respondents selected this category (ranging from 50.0% to 67.5%). In contrast, for nonsepsis-related emergencies, a significantly smaller proportion (between 23.2% and 51.2%) chose this response option. Furthermore, we found that a noticeable proportion of participants would not use EMC, even if they classified the medical situation as very urgent ( Fig. ). On average, this proportion was significantly higher for sepsis-related emergencies (mean = 35%) than for nonsepsis-related emergencies (mean = 17%). A detailed description of the intended actions by vignette can be found in Figure S1 ( https://links.lww.com/CCM/H850 ). In the multiple regression for the urgency rating of sepsis-related case vignettes ( Table ), only a comparably small proportion of 8.8% of the variance was explained ( R 2 = 0.088), with sepsis knowledge as the only significant predictor, while age, sex, education, and previous experience with sepsis were no significant explanatory variables in this model. Regarding the multiple regression for the tendency to use EMC ( Table ), the perceived urgency was the strongest predictor controlling for all other predictors. The likelihood of EMC use in sepsis-related emergencies was significantly lower compared with nonsepsis-related emergencies (–14.9%; p < 0.01). Among the possible barriers to utilization of EMC, only “long waiting times in the ED” was a significant predictor. Age, sex, and education had no association with the tendency to use EMC. In total, 37.1% of the variance of tendency to use EMC is explained by the set of predictor variables ( R 2 = 0.371). The rating of the perceived urgency of sepsis-related emergencies was only associated with sepsis knowledge, while sociodemographic factors and previous sepsis experience had no significant impact. DISCUSSION In this representative survey, respondents rated the urgency of sepsis-related medical emergencies lower compared with nonsepsis-related emergencies. The rating of the perceived urgency of sepsis-related emergencies was only associated with sepsis knowledge, while sociodemographic factors and previous sepsis experience had no significant impact. Notably, controlling for the perceived urgency, respondents chose EMC less frequently in sepsis-related urgencies. Our results align with previous studies showing a positive association between perceived urgency and the decision to seek EMS or ED care, regardless of specific diagnoses ( ). We expand this research and the evidence of our previous study ( ) by showing that the type of emergency is associated with the tendency of EMC use, even if controlling for the perceived urgency. In that regard, sepsis-related emergencies are associated with a lower tendency for EMC use, which may contribute to delays in treatment of this time-sensitive emergency with potential increases in sepsis mortality. We lack data to understand why patients who rated a vignette as highly urgent were less likely to choose EMC for sepsis-related cases than for nonseptic cases in our study. In another case vignette study, the “certainty” of choice influenced the likelihood to seek medical services ( ). It may be possible that respondents’ certainty of the need for medical treatment is greater for AMI and stroke than for sepsis. To this end, even health providers highlight that the low specificity of sepsis symptoms is hindering themselves from early sepsis diagnoses and communication in qualitative interviews ( ). Also in public, sepsis symptoms seem to be less known than typical AMI or stroke symptoms ( – ). This is supported by a German study in which EMS patients were much more likely “not” to choose an EMS for a vignette with “high fever for several days” (adverting sepsis) compared with a vignette with “tight chest pain” (indicating AMI) ( ). Furthermore, it is possible that previous awareness campaigns for stroke and AMI have resulted in a higher level of awareness in the population and possibly perceived susceptibility of patients, although it was shown that sepsis incidence in EMS is similar to AMI and stroke incidence ( ). In addition, the preference for consulting a GP rather than using EMC in sepsis-related emergencies may reflect the more gradual and less specific onset of typical sepsis symptoms compared with the sudden and clearly recognizable presentations of stroke or AMI. This relative ambiguity may reinforce the perception that immediate EMC is not required, even when respondents rate the situation as highly urgent. However, further research is needed to understand the comparatively lower tendency to use EMC in highly urgent sepsis-like emergencies. Our study identified factors that are associated with the perceived urgency of sepsis-related emergencies. While sociodemographic characteristics had no impact, the respondents’ sepsis knowledge was the most important predictor of the perceived urgency. However, with regard to sepsis knowledge, large gaps exist in the general population and at-risk patients ( ). According to healthcare providers interviewed in a German mixed methods study, patients’ sepsis education is currently considered inferior compared with education on other diseases ( ). This is in line with a study from Korea that found a lower awareness for sepsis compared with stroke and AMI ( ). The public’s low sepsis knowledge may also be partially due to the fact that sepsis is—different to AMI and stroke—a syndrome, thus, often only communicated/known as the underlying infection, for example, an urinary infection, without the word “sepsis” being used ( ). It may reflect the fact that AMI and stroke have been recognized and researched for much longer and have therefore been the focus of public awareness campaigns for decades, whereas broader recognition of sepsis has only emerged more recently. It may also contribute to this lower awareness that, unlike AMI or stroke, sepsis is not clearly linked to a single medical specialty that actively promotes awareness or serves as a direct point of reference for the public. Furthermore, sepsis does not appear to be consistently documented in discharge letters of affected patients ( ). The importance of sepsis knowledge for rating the urgency of sepsis underlines the necessity of comprehensive public sepsis education, which might also unfold its potential with regard to correct identification of symptoms of life-threatening infection and timely EMC seeking. This claim is also a major demand of a call for the development of a European sepsis plan just recently issued by sepsis survivors ( ). The importance of sepsis knowledge for rating the urgency of sepsis underlines the necessity of comprehensive public sepsis education, which might also unfold its potential with regard to correct identification of symptoms of life-threatening infection and timely EMC seeking. This claim is also a major demand of a call for the development of a European sepsis plan just recently issued by sepsis survivors ( ). In Germany, there are already several initiatives such as World Sepsis Day, the nationwide campaign “Deutschland erkennt Sepsis” (Germany recognizes sepsis), and scientific public health projects in model regions (e.g., Strengthening health literacy of patients at high risk for sepsis in order to improve early diagnosis and treatment of sepsis [SEPWISS]) ( ). However, these activities have so far not been sufficient to reach the general population on a broad scale. Strengthening sepsis-related emergency competence as part of overall health literacy therefore remains essential and requires stronger efforts. Furthermore, training of medical professionals and students, who themselves often show limited knowledge ( , ), represents another crucial element to disseminate sepsis awareness more effectively. Beyond these efforts, better data and visibility of sepsis are also required to raise awareness at both professional and societal levels. This includes consistent documentation of sepsis in discharge summaries, explicit coding of sepsis on death certificates, and the establishment of national surveillance systems to more accurately capture the burden of disease ( ). Such measures are in line with the World Health Organization Global Sepsis Resolution ( ), including public awareness as a key priority. Another important finding is that the perceived urgency is the major driver for the tendency to use emergency care, and barriers only play a minor role. Among the barriers, only long waiting times in the ED were associated with a decreased tendency for EMC seeking. This barrier was also highlighted in a previous qualitative study on barriers to seeking care for symptoms of bacterial sepsis ( ) and emerged as major barrier in studies on the seeking care in the ED for other medical emergencies ( ). In contrast to findings from U.S. studies ( ), fear of costs or mobility-related barriers were not significantly associated with the tendency to use EMC in our study. This may be due to differences in the healthcare system with compulsory health insurance for all citizens, low costs for EMS use (usually 10 Euros per transport and 10 Euros per day hospitalization) and comparably short distances to hospitals with EDs in Germany ( ). This study is among the first to use case vignettes to analyze perceived urgency, intended actions, and barriers to EMC use, comparing sepsis with nonsepsis-related emergencies. Its representative sample enables generalizable results for the German population and expands the literature by focusing on reasons for not seeking emergency care, whereas most prior studies examined emergency overuse and overcrowding ( ). However, our study has also limitations. Case vignettes represent a thought experiment, and it is possible that the respondents would act differently if they actually experienced the symptoms described in the case vignettes themselves. Furthermore, as our vignettes used typical AMI and stroke symptoms, it may be possible that we overestimated the respondents’ ability to identify the correct actions for those emergencies, which also can present with less specific symptoms, for example, in patients with diabetes or the elderly. Furthermore, information on participants’ occupational background, including potential employment in healthcare, was not collected and could therefore not be considered in our analyses, although this may influence the ability to assess medical emergencies. A further limitation is that information on the total number of individuals approached and on incomplete interviews was not provided by the survey institute, which restricts the assessment of response rates and potential selection bias. Finally, the survey may not have captured all relevant barriers to seeking emergency care, particularly system-level factors such as access, availability, or perceived capacity of EMS. Although we included items approximating this aspect (e.g., concerns about disadvantaging other patients), broader structural barriers may not be fully reflected. CONCLUSIONS While barriers play a secondary role in the decision to use EMC, the decisive factor is the perceived urgency of the emergency, which, in the case of sepsis, also depends on knowledge of the disease. Given the rather low level of sepsis knowledge in the general population, this emphasizes the potential and the need for an increase sepsis knowledge in public, with a specific focus on sepsis symptoms and the awareness that sepsis requires timely emergency care. Introduction New onset status epilepticus (NORSE) and its subcategory Febrile Infection Related Encephalopathy Syndrome (FIRES) have been described in adult and pediatric patients under various terms starting as early as 1950's. The term NORSE was coined by Wilder-Smith in 2005; the definition and clinical criteria were formalized in 2018 ( – ). NORSE encompasses various clinical presentations of de novo recurrent refractory seizures without evidence of acute structural, metabolic, or toxic causes ( ). The true incidence of NORSE is unknown; however, it may constitute up to 20% of all cases of refractory status epilepticus ( , ). NORSE most frequently occurs in previously healthy young adults and school-aged children; however, older individuals, including septuagenarians, have also been affected. In adult case series, a higher prevalence has been reported in women. This contrasts with pediatric case series where NORSE predominantly affects boys ( , – ). An etiology is identified in up to 50% of the adult patients with NORSE, most of whom suffer from primary or paraneoplastic autoimmune encephalitis ( ). On the other hand, paraneoplastic and autoimmune NORSE is rare in children ( – ). A prodromal phase has been reported in 60–100% of patients with NORSE. The prodrome precedes the onset of seizures and status epilepticus (SE) by 1–14 days ( – , ) and includes fever, a cardinal diagnostic criterion of FIRES, in 34–91% of patients ( – ). Other prodromal symptoms include headache, mild gastrointestinal or upper respiratory illness, and behavioral disturbances ( , ). Electroencephalogram (EEG) abnormalities are present in all NORSE patients, and seizures are detected in more than 88% of patients undergoing continuous video EEG monitoring ( , ). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as well as laboratory examination of serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for the presence of autoantibodies or abnormal immunoglobulin indexes are routinely performed and are frequently abnormal ( – ). Strides have been made in evidence-based care for NORSE patients. Criteria for the diagnosis of NORSE has been introduced and accepted by the neurology community ( ). In addition, evidence- and experience-based recommendations for the management of patients with NORSE have been published by experts from the International NORSE Consensus Group ( , ). While significant progress has been made in delineating the diagnostic and treatment approaches for NORSE, less emphasis has been placed on studying clinical outcomes, including the long-term sequalae, after the hospital discharge. Further, the literature focuses primarily on seizure outcomes, as refractory epilepsy represents the most significant disability in survivors of NORSE ( , , – , – ). However, over two-thirds of patients experience moderate to severe cognitive disability following hospitalization or remain in a vegetative state ( , , , , ). Reports concerning functional limitations after NORSE are sparse and include components of formal functional assessment or narrative descriptions of impaired academic performance or activities of daily living ( , , – , – ). The emergence of psychiatric and behavioral disturbances after NORSE have also been described; however, the full spectrum of these complications have not been systematically assessed outside of the time of hospitalization. In this study, we conducted a systematic review of literature on NORSE and compiled data on the neurological and psychiatric outcomes of NORSE at 30 or more days following hospitalization. The long-term outcomes of SE and refractory SE have been documented in recent systematic reviews where the patient symptoms were assessed starting as early as 30 days after the discharge ( – ). Consistent with previously set criteria ( – ), we considered to use a 30-day mark as an appropriate interval after which the outcomes of SE were considered “long-term.” Given that some of these complications may improve over time, we did not restrict the length of follow-up after hospitalization in these reports. We disaggregated the findings in adult and pediatric patients and summarized the key demographic and clinical features of these cohorts. The purpose of this systematic review is to tackle the special circumstance of de-novo SE and highlight the spectrum of neurocognitive disabilities in patient recovering from NORSE. 2. Methods The systematic review protocol was developed using guidance from the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement ( ) and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, Center for Reviews and Dissemination number CRD42022361142) ( ). 2.1. Search strategy Literature searches were initially carried out from May 30–June 1, 2021, and later updated with the final update on October 13, 2022. MEDLINE (EBSCOhost), CINAHL (EBSCOhost), APAPsycINFO (EBSCOhost), EMBASE ( embase.com , version including 1974-present), Scopus, and the Cochrane Library (including the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, wiley.com ) were searched from inception to the final search date. The search strategy was developed by a librarian (C.S.) in consultation with epileptologist with research interest in neuroimmunology and clinical subspecialty in autoimmune epilepsy (O.T.). Each database search included terms representing the “long-term follow-up” and “NORSE” concepts (see complete search strategies available at https://digitalcommons.unmc.edu/search/14 ). The “long-term follow-up” concept was represented by a variety of subject headings and keywords. Since none of the databases we used had a subject heading for the “NORSE” concept, this concept was represented by keywords and key phrases alone. The following alternate names and acronyms for NORSE were considered during search strategy development: new-onset refractory status epilepticus, NORSE, febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome, FIRES, febrile illness-related epilepsy, fever-induced refractory epileptic encephalopathy, idiopathic catastrophic epileptic encephalopathy, severe refractory status epilepticus owing to presumed encephalitis, devastating epilepsy in school-age children, DESC, acute non-herpetic encephalitis with refractory repetitive partial seizures, acute encephalitis with refractory repetitive partial seizures, AERRPS, de novo cryptogenic refractory multifocal febrile status epilepticus. The search strategies were designed to retrieve records containing any of these names listed and to retrieve records containing any of the listed acronyms if the record in question also contained a word beginning with one of the following word trunks: epilep, convul, or seizur. Since no funds were available for translation, English- language filters were applied. Conference abstracts, editorials, and review articles were separated from other search results when filters allowed. 2.2. Study selection and quality assessment The database searches retrieved 3,261 total records (142 from CINAHL, 24 from the Cochrane Library, 637 from EMBASE, 911 from MEDLINE, 306 from PsycINFO and 1,241 from Scopus, ). All search results were imported into RefWorks and 1,659 duplicate records were removed using RefWorks' and Zotero duplicate detection tools. A total of 1,602 unique publications remained for title/abstract review ( ). The titles and abstracts were reviewed by two independent neurologists (S.P. and N.G.) for the inclusion criteria and selected articles were chosen for full review. Disagreements between reviewers and inquiries by reviewers were resolved by another reviewer. Reports on other types of SE that did not fulfill the criteria of NORSE as well as those with outcomes reported at <30 days following the discharge were excluded. Case reports and case series were evaluated based on completeness and quality of reporting and were excluded if they did not provide the pertinent information ( ). 2.3. Data extraction Data extraction was performed using a standardized template. In addition to basic demographic data, the following outcomes were extracted: duration of follow-up, proportion of patients with seizures controlled with anti-seizure medications (ASM) or other treatments, proportion of patients with refractory seizures and recurrent SE, presence and severity of acquired cognitive disability with specific reference to memory impairment. In addition, functional outcomes assessed with Modified Rankin Scale (mRS), Clinical Global Impressions of Improvement Scale (CGI-I), Pediatric Cerebral Performance Score (PCPS), or Glasgow outcome score (GOS) at the last follow-up visit and proportion of patients with acquired neurological comorbidities, psychiatric complications, and learning disabilities were extracted. 2.4. Data analysis Age was determined through weighted means, when possible. The sex distribution, proportions of patients with seizures, SE, cognitive failure, and other comorbidities were assessed when possible. Comparisons of results between the age groups were descriptive only and not statistically assessed. The summaries were disaggregated for the adult patients (19 years and older), the children, and the mixed age cohort. Given that the age range of patients in the individual reports was broad, the outcomes for various age groups could not be stratified. Similarly, given that the range of follow-up time was broad in the individual reports and these intervals were largely non-overlapping, the outcomes for the specific time intervals were not assessed. 3. Results 3.1. Demographic patient characteristics From 1,602 publications identified by the search, 1,389 reports were excluded after the initial title and abstract screening as they did not meet criteria for NORSE/refractory status epilepticus (RSE), and 213 reports were selected for full manuscript review ( ). Demographic patient characteristics From 1,602 publications identified by the search, 1,389 reports were excluded after the initial title and abstract screening as they did not meet criteria for NORSE/refractory status epilepticus (RSE), and 213 reports were selected for full manuscript review ( ). Of these 213 articles, 33 studies in adults and 52 studies in children met the inclusion criteria ( ). Three reports contained findings for adult and pediatric age groups. Collectively, the reports contained a description of 280 adult and 587 pediatric patients of which the data on the long-term seizure and cognitive outcomes were available for 212 (75.7 %) adult and 499 (85%) pediatric patients, respectively. In two studies that did not disaggregate findings by age (166 patients total), the data on long-term outcomes were available in 127 (76.5%) patients ( , ). In the adult group, the mean age of patients was 34.3 years, and the majority (77.6%) were female. The working diagnosis of NORSE was established in 146 (68.9%) patients, FIRES in 9 (4.3%) patients, new onset super refractory SE (NOSRSE) in 17 (8%) patients, RSE and superrefractory SE (SRSE) in 17 (8%) patients, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in 2 (0.9%) patients, unspecified autoimmune encephalitis in 19 (8.9%) patients, and acute encephalitis with repetitive recurrent partial seizures (AERRPS) or presumed limbic encephalitis in 2 (0.9%) patients. Pertinent laboratory findings in these patients included the autoantibodies against NMDA receptors (28), GABA A receptors (1), GABA B receptors (2), voltage gated potassium channel complex (VGKC, 7), contactin-associated-protein (CASPR,1), type 1 anti-neuronal nuclear protein (ANNA-1, anti-Hu, 1) and GAD-65 proteins (8) in the serum or CSF; however, the tumor status of patients was not consistently recorded. In the large case series on NORSE, paraneoplastic antibodies in patients with confirmed malignancies included anti-Ro (1), anti- NMDA receptor (9), anti-VGKC (3), anti-Hu (3), anti-voltage gated calcium channel (VGCC, 2) antibodies and collapsing response mediator protein 5 (CRMP-5, 1) ( ). Collectively, the etiology of NORSE appeared to be established in 37.7% of 106 patients described in articles meeting our inclusion criteria. Other findings in adult patients were signal abnormalities on the MRI (4) or mass spectroscopy (1) of the brain. In pediatric studies, the mean age of patients was 7.9 years, and 42.5 % were female. The diagnosis of NORSE or FIRES were established in 149 (29.8%) and 237 (47.4 %) of patients, respectively. The pertinent findings in patients' evaluation included presence of autoantibodies in the serum and CSF specimens in 19 (3.2%) patients. The antibodies against NMDA receptors (2), GABA A receptors (1), AMPA-GluR3 receptors (1), and GAD-65 protein (6) as well as elevated serum and CSF anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies (1) were documented along with the increase of CSF cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor and interleukins 6 and 10 (1). Genetic deficiencies (5) and secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (3) were also recorded as the possible etiologies of NORSE. Brain MRI examinations were abnormal in 31 patients and revealed various degrees of cortical atrophy (10), signal changes in the claustrum (1), temporal cortical regions (2), and cerebellum (1) as well as bilateral hippocampal atrophy (1). In two large reports that collectively included 127 adult and pediatric patients, the proportion of female patients was smaller than male (41.7%); but the age of participants was not consistently provided ( , ). The autoimmune antibodies were not identified in serum and CSF of these patients. The cortical and hippocampal signal abnormalities on brain MRI were reported in 27 patients. 3.2. Cognitive outcomes Cognitive outcomes at 30 days or later following the hospital discharge were reported for 22 (10.4%) of the adult patients included in the reviewed literature; most of these patients were described in case reports ( ). Most of the studies assessed cognitive outcomes subjectively. All available data on neuropsychological testing, including the formal test scores are provided in , . At the last follow-up, 3 patients (13.6%) had normal cognition, 2 (9.1%) had mild cognitive impairment, and 4 (18.2%) and 2 (9.1%) had moderate or severe degrees of cognitive impairment, respectively. Three patients (13.6%) remained in a vegetative state; however, the time of assessment (10 months) was only documented for one patient. Memory impairment was reported in 12 patients (54.5%). Four (33.3%) of these had moderate or severe impairment. Specific reference to working or visual memory impairments were made in 2 patients. Mild naming deficits (1) and persistent impairment of processing speed and verbal memory function (1) were also reported at the last follow-up. Reports concerning pediatric patients elaborated on cognitive outcomes after hospital discharge more frequently than reports concerning adults. The assessment of cognitive status was documented in 68.9% of all 344 included pediatric patients with NORSE ( , ). Seventy-eight patients (22.7%) have experienced complete cognitive recovery. Mild impairment was diagnosed in 42 children (12.2%), while moderate and severe loss were noted in 60 (17.4%) and 50 (14.5%) of children, respectively. Thirty patients (8.7%) have remained in a vegetative state. The degree of intellectual disability was not specified in 94 (27.3%) children. References to specific memory impairment were made in reports concerning 19 patients of whom 8 had a severe memory loss. Delayed motor, social, and verbal development were noted in 1 child described in a case report. 3.4. Acquired psychiatric comorbidities and neurological deficits The emergence of new onset psychiatric disorders in adult survivors of NORSE were reported in only 7 (3.3%) patients ( ). These manifestations included schizophrenia (1), attention deficit disorder (2), Capgras syndrome (1), psychomotor agitation (1), and personality changes (2). Various neurological deficits were reported in 6 patients and included bilateral lower extremity weakness and mild ataxia (1), right hemiparesis and dysphasia (1), mild receptive dysphasia (1), and moderate language impairment (1) as well as unspecified gait disturbance (1). The description of psychiatric complications of NORSE were more common in the pediatric literature and were provided for 56 (11.2%) of all included children ( ). Reports concerning 56 of the pediatric patients mentioned behavioral disturbances of various severity: 13 developed aggression, 2 suffered from emotional lability, 4 had apathy, and 1 had conduct disorder. Mild or severe attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and various manifestations of attention impairment were diagnosed in 9 patients and an autism spectrum disorder was reported in 1 patient. One child attempted suicide. Various neurological sequalae of NORSE were described in 108 (21.6%) children. Specifically, the long-term motor deficits included hemiplegia (35, 32.4%), unspecified motor impairments (36, 33.3%) and unilateral tongue weakness (1, 0.01%). Other impairments included visual field deficits (1), peripheral neuropathy (2), ataxia (3), choreoathetoid movements (1), and tremor (3). Language deficits were reported in 20 (18.5%) patients. One of these children improved after the initiation of responsive neurostimulation. 4. Discussion In the present study, we systematically reviewed and summarized the literature on the long-term neurological and psychiatric outcomes of NORSE in adult and pediatric patients who survived longer than 30 days after hospital discharge. We found that seizure status is assessed in over 90% of patients who had the data on the long-term outcomes. However, the cognitive outcomes were only included in one tenth of these reports in adults and nearly two-thirds of the reports concerning children. Functional outcomes were included in more than 60% of studies of adults and more than 25 % of studies of children. Unfortunately, the functional outcomes were measured using four different outcome scales limiting our ability to synthesize study results into an understanding of the overall scope of associated disability. New onset psychiatric disorders were under-reported and were only included in a small proportion of the reports. Overall, these findings reflect the lack of standardization for the reporting of outcomes, particularly for reporting symptoms other than seizures, and may also reflect a gap in the care of these patients after the initial hospital encounters. 4.1. hospital encounters. 4.1. Seizure outcomes Consistent with previous observations, in this systematic review, we found that majority of adults and children with NORSE will continue to have seizures 30 days or later after the hospital discharge. Of those who continue to have seizures, 41.1% of adults and 57.7% of children will remain refractory to either conventional ASDs used alone or in combination with immunotherapies, ketogenic diet, and neurostimulation. The pathogenesis of recurrent seizures in NORSE is not clear. Several proposed mechanisms of uncontrolled seizure generation during the acute phase of NORSE included aberrant signaling in the interleukin (IL)-1 and toll-like receptor (TLR)-mediated pathways, overactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome as well as functional or genetic deficiency of IL-1 receptor antagonist activity ( , , – ). These mechanisms can also be involved in late seizure recurrence in survivors of NORSE. Of note, chronic epilepsy in cryptogenic NORSE develops without a latent period which is distinct from the post-infectious epilepsies associated with viral or bacterial pathogens ( , ). 4.2. Cognitive outcomes Our findings add to those of previous studies that showed only a small proportion of patients have achieved their pre-morbid cognitive function after they were discharged from the hospital ( ). Nearly one-third of adults or children continue to suffer from moderate and severe intellectual disability. In a case series of 14 pediatric patients with NORSE, all children attended special education in the later course, and seven patients had severe cognitive failure. The primary impairment involved deficits in frontal lobe function and was manifesting as the lack of motor and speech initiative, major slowness, perseveration, and poor attention ( , ). While there were no specific patterns in neuropathological findings in NORSE, gliosis, laminar cortical necrosis, and diffuse cortical atrophy are the shared common features ( , , , , ). Moreover, various degrees of persistent inflammation and structural changes such as mesial temporal sclerosis may contribute to the severity of cognitive phenotype. Chronic cognitive disability after NORSE represents the major public health problem. Since many patients are previously healthy, severe cognitive impairment or vegetative states after NORSE are devastating. A need exists for comprehensive chronic care that includes cognitive rehabilitation for patients and respite for caregivers. The mechanism of cognitive failure in NORSE is unclear, but it is likely linked to the severity and duration of seizures ( ). In subtypes of autoimmune encephalitis that can manifest as NORSE (e.g., anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis), antibodies were found to be directly pathogenic for memory failure and seizures. However, the pathogenesis of epileptic encephalopathy in other antibody-mediated or cryptogenic NORSE is not clear ( , , ). The lack of the uniformed objective measurements of cognitive function noted in the reviewed literature represents a major shortcoming of this research. More systematic and comprehensive objective testing of survivals is needed in future studies. 4.3. Functional outcomes and activities of daily living We found that a comprehensive approach in documenting the functional outcomes in survivors of NORSE were lacking. Further, only one-fourth of the children and 60% of adults in our study had their functional outcomes assessed and reported. While the mRS was the most common outcome scale applied in adult patients, there were three additional outcomes scales used in pediatric patients. Such inconsistent data availability in outcomes particularly for the pediatric patients introduce a potential bias and limits definitive conclusions. In the recent systematic analysis of functional outcomes in autoimmune encephalitis, it was established that mRS had poor sensitivity for cognitive disability and mood disturbances in encephalitis at follow-up ( ). There was an additional focus on the academic performance and other aspects of social functioning in children, which were consistently underreported in the adult literature. Given that many patients with NORSE have now survived for several decades, a more standardized approach in categorization of their functional abilities is needed to monitor their recovery and develop guidelines for individualized rehabilitation. 4.4. Acquired psychiatric comorbidities and neurological deficits Psychiatric comorbidities, including recurrent psychosis are frequently encountered in severe epileptic encephalopathies ( ); however, the prevalence of mental illness in association with recent refractory SE is unknown. Multiple factors could contribute to the development of psychosis and depression in patients recovering from NORSE, including the individual vulnerability to the effects of ASDs or immunotherapy as well as prolonged brain hypoxia ( ). The presence of specific autoimmune antibodies (such as anti-AMPA or anti-NMDA receptor antibodies) in NORSE with established etiologies can guide the anticipation of chronic psychiatric sequalae ( ). The accounts of new onset psychiatric disorders in only 3.3 and 11.2% of the adults and pediatric patients with chronic NORSE likely reflects underreporting and insufficient attention to these comorbidities on the part of neurologists involved in care of these patients. 4.5. Limitations Our study has several limitations. We found that the majority of reports on long-term outcomes of NORSE are focused on seizure status while other domains of the neurological and psychiatric health were assessed and commented on inconsistently. This likely represents a reporting bias and underreporting in various relevant health domains for the most severely disabled patients (e.g., those in vegetative state) and those whose seizures were under better control. This limits our conclusions regarding the prevalence of multiple manifestations of chronic NORSE other than seizures. Given the retrospective and observational design of most reviewed studies, it is unclear whether the severity of SE and its refractoriness can be linked to any of the reported outcomes. This impedes our progress in understanding the mechanisms of cognitive failure and development of psychiatric comorbidities in NORSE. Given that the analysis in specific age categories in pediatric patients was not feasible, the outcomes of SE at different stages of brain development and the effects of age-related compensatory abilities have not been accounted for. Likewise, the inability to disaggregate the data into the specific duration of follow-up precluded the analysis of outcomes at different stages of recovery from NORSE. Lastly, we acknowledge the selection and information bias that was not specifically assessed in this systematic review. 5. Conclusions We found that most patients with chronic NORSE continue to experience recurrent seizures, and seizure treatment and reporting remain the main focus of the literature. Documentation of cognitive disability, loss of functional independence, and onset psychiatric manifestations have been inconsistent and should be interpreted with caution given the methodological limitations. While challenging to implement due to the rarity and geographic dispersion of NORSE, future prospective studies may help provide high-quality evidence to guide the management and rehabilitation of these patients.
